questions.q: What problem is the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator specifically designed to solve?
options: Projecting the physical qubits and runtime an algorithm would need on future fault-tolerant hardware, before that hardware exists
Running a program on today's noisy real hardware faster than the normal queue
Automatically fixing bugs in Q# source code
Converting Q# programs into Qiskit circuits
questions.explain: The resource estimator exists to answer hardware/algorithm co-design and feasibility questions years before fault-tolerant hardware is actually built, not to execute or optimize programs on existing hardware.

questions.q: What does a resource estimator job return, as opposed to what a simulator job returns?
options: A histogram of measurement outcomes, identical to a simulator
A structured report of physical qubits required, runtime, logical qubits needed, and error budget -- not measurement results
The exact source code of a more efficient version of the algorithm
A list of real hardware providers currently online
questions.explain: Unlike a simulator (which returns measurement outcomes), the resource estimator returns a hardware-requirements projection: physical qubit count, runtime, logical qubit count, and error budget breakdown.

questions.q: What are 'qubit parameters' in the context of the resource estimator?
options: The names of the qubits in your Q# code
Configurable assumptions about future hardware -- qubit technology, error rates, error-correction code parameters -- that the estimator uses to produce its projection
The number of shots requested for a simulator run
A fixed, unchangeable setting built into every Azure Quantum workspace
questions.explain: Qubit parameters are exactly the configurable hardware assumptions (technology, error rates, code distance) you supply, letting you ask 'what if the hardware were better in this specific way' without that hardware existing yet.

questions.q: In the lesson's illustrative calculation using physical qubits per logical qubit ~ 2 x d^2 with d=15, what was the computed and verified result for 6 logical qubits?
options: 450 total physical qubits
2,700 total physical qubits (450 per logical qubit x 6 logical qubits)
90 total physical qubits
15 total physical qubits
questions.explain: 2 x 15^2 = 450 physical qubits per logical qubit; multiplied by 6 illustrative logical qubits gives 2,700 -- explicitly framed as a simplified illustrative calculation, not a real estimator output.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this capability has no direct equivalent in the Qiskit ecosystem?
options: Qiskit's transpilation/gate-count analysis tools target near-term circuit optimization, not a standardized, integrated, vendor-agnostic fault-tolerant hardware-requirements projection built into the core toolchain
Qiskit cannot analyze circuits in any way
Qiskit requires a paid subscription for any form of circuit analysis
IBM has never published any research on resource estimation
questions.explain: The distinction is about integration and standardization: Qiskit has circuit-depth/gate-count analysis for near-term circuits, but not a single first-class, push-button, vendor-agnostic fault-tolerant resource-estimation service built into the core toolchain the way Azure Quantum's is.
